title: The One With Phoebes Wedding

jokes.text: Girls in my magazine are a lot nakeder.
jokes.setup: Joey is flipping through a magazine, implying it might be a bridal or wedding publication
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals he's comparing it unfavorably to his usual pornographic magazines, delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open. The word 'nakeder' (a Joey malapropism) and the complete guilelessness of comparing a bridal magazine to porn is quintessential Joey character comedy. High character integration — only Joey would say this with such earnest sincerity. Economy is excellent; the whole joke is six words.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My stepdad can't get weekend furlough for my wedding because he stabbed a guy in the prison library.

jokes.text: Well, apparently stabbing Iceman in the exercise yard couldn't wait till Monday.
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains her stepdad got a prison furlough to attend the wedding but then called with bad news
jokes.punchline: He shanked a fellow inmate named 'Iceman' and therefore can't make it — delivered by Phoebe with breezy nonchalance as if this is a minor scheduling conflict
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specificity of 'Iceman' (a prison nickname that implies a whole underworld hierarchy), the absurd logic that this 'couldn't wait till Monday,' and Phoebe's total calm all combine beautifully. It's dark, it's character-integrated (Phoebe's chaotic backstory is a running element of the show), and 'couldn't wait till Monday' is a killer construction — framing a stabbing as a procrastination failure. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You've shared your wisdom with me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I'm wisdomous.

jokes.text: I am pretty 'wisdomous.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Joey he has 'shared his wisdom' with her, as flattery before asking him to walk her down the aisle
jokes.punchline: Joey coins a fake word — 'wisdomous' — with complete sincerity, treating it as a real compliment to himself
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey malapropism/neologism. 'Wisdomous' is a perfect invented word — it sounds almost right, which makes it funnier than a completely wrong word would. High character integration because this is Joey's defining verbal tic. Economy is perfect at three words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Go to your room.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Just go to your room so you won't see me cry.

jokes.text: I don't want you to see your father cry. Go to your room!
jokes.setup: Joey is visibly getting emotional after Phoebe calls him a father figure and they share a sweet moment; he begins saying 'I hope you know...' twice but can't finish
jokes.punchline: Instead of completing his emotional thought, Joey suddenly snaps into a fake-dad authoritarian mode and banishes Phoebe from the room to hide his tears
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the setup has Joey fumbling toward an emotional declaration twice, building genuine warmth, then it pivots into absurdist comedy-dad bluster. 'Go to your room!' is a great punchline because it both deflects the emotion and plays into the father-figure role Phoebe just assigned him. High quotability and genuine character work. Very close to an 8 on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, no, no! The sea bass is too dry. We need the salmon. The salmon is moist and—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Monica, they hung up on you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? They can't hang up on me! I was in the middle of a sentence!

jokes.text: Oh, no, no, no. Let your dad get this.
jokes.setup: Monica's phone rings with another wedding crisis call; Joey is now playing his new 'dad' role earnestly
jokes.punchline: Joey intercepts the call as if he's literally Phoebe's father, telling her to 'let your dad get this' — fully committing to the bit
jokes.explanation: A quick, solid callback to the father-figure dynamic. Joey fully committing to the paternal role is funny but doesn't add new dimension — it's largely coasting on the setup from the prior scene.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'll meet you at 1900 hours.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: 1900 hours? What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's 7 PM in military time.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh, well sorry, I wasn't in missile training.

jokes.text: I must have been in missile training the day they taught that.
jokes.setup: Monica, acting as drill-sergeant wedding planner, asks Joey if he knows military time (1800 hours). He doesn't.
jokes.punchline: Joey sarcastically suggests he was busy with 'missile training' on the day military time was taught — a deadpan absurdist excuse that punctures Monica's military cosplay
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback. 'Missile training' is the right level of absurd — specific enough to be funny, broad enough to land immediately. It also works as character comedy for Joey (he's not in the military but improvises plausible-sounding nonsense) and gently mocks Monica's over-the-top military wedding-planner persona.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Subtract 12 from 1800 to get 6 PM.

jokes.text: Okay, so 1800 minus 12... is 1788.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Joey to 'just subtract 12' to convert military time
jokes.punchline: Joey literally subtracts 12 from 1800 and arrives at 1788, treating it as a valid answer
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey-is-dumb joke. It works because the audience sees it coming half a beat before Joey lands it, which creates the satisfying 'of course' laugh. The setup is clean and the execution is fast. Not wildly original — this type of Joey math joke has appeared in the series before — but it's well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, Marjorie smells so bad, I'm thinking by the time she takes a bath, Tibet will be independent.

jokes.text: Ice sculpture? That sounds really fancy. I told you, I just want a simple wedding.
jokes.setup: Monica is orchestrating an elaborate wedding with ice sculptures, harpists, and meticulous planning
jokes.punchline: Phoebe protests she wanted a 'simple wedding' — the irony being that an ice sculpture is the least of Monica's extravagances, and Monica's response is to steamroll her completely
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy built on the Monica-as-control-freak dynamic. It's not a sharp joke so much as a reliable character beat that keeps the Monica subplot moving. Gets a mild laugh from the Monica/Phoebe dynamic but doesn't transcend.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A rehearsal dinner? So we're just gonna practice eating?

jokes.text: She will shower when Tibet is free.
jokes.setup: Monica fired Phoebe's friend Marjorie (the steel drums player) in part because of Marjorie's 'overwhelming scent.' Phoebe defends her.
jokes.punchline: Monica dismisses Marjorie's hygiene with the kicker that she's on a principled political protest — she won't shower until Tibet is liberated, which Monica delivers as if it perfectly explains and settles the matter
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuinely exceptional jokes. The punchline is completely unexpected, hyper-specific, and contains a whole character (Marjorie) in one line. The Tibet reference situates it in a very particular late-90s/early-2000s activist culture, which gives it texture. Monica's total nonchalance ('She will shower when Tibet is free' — not even a question) is the perfect deadpan delivery note. High quotability; this is the kind of line that gets repeated. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh, we're hugging?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your hands are on my butt.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: I'm glad we're having a rehearsal dinner. I rarely practice my meals before I eat.
jokes.setup: Characters arrive at the rehearsal dinner; Ross comments on being glad they're having one
jokes.punchline: Ross plays on 'rehearsal dinner' — treating it as if 'rehearsing' your dinner (the food) is a thing one might literally do
jokes.explanation: A competent wordplay joke on 'rehearsal dinner.' It's the kind of pun that gets an 'ugh, fine' chuckle — the setup is obvious and the wordplay isn't particularly fresh. It also doesn't feel especially Ross-specific; most characters could deliver it. Functional but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why are you so sad about your baby? It's not like it's dead or anything.

jokes.text: No stupid jokes, but I thought that was for the actual wedding. / Rehearse it.
jokes.setup: Monica told Ross his one gift to the couple was 'no stupid jokes.' Ross assumed this only applied to the wedding itself.
jokes.punchline: Monica's one-word 'Rehearse it' — meaning he should practice not making stupid jokes at the rehearsal dinner — is a perfect deadpan snap
jokes.explanation: Monica's 'Rehearse it' is brilliantly economical — two words that also retroactively comment on Ross's joke we just heard. It functions as a meta-callback: the audience realizes Monica's directive is a response to the pun we just witnessed. Very tight construction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: 20 seconds per person. That's it. In, hug, out.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We have 200 guests and a timeline. Let's move, people!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What are you doing? You're at 45 seconds with Mrs. Geller's cousin. You're wasting time!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're all clowns! Inefficient clowns!

jokes.text: I was going for a handshake. / That why your hand's against my crotch?
jokes.setup: Chandler goes to greet Mike; there's an awkward physical confusion about whether to hug or handshake
jokes.punchline: Mike points out that in Chandler's confusion, his hand ended up against Mike's crotch — which Chandler calmly confirms was his handshake attempt
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy beat that works better visually than it reads on the page. The awkward male-greeting genre is familiar territory, and landing on 'crotch' is the obvious escalation. The humor is in Chandler's deadpan confirmation ('That is why') but doesn't reach beyond a solid mid-tier laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mike's Father
dialogue.line: You think you know about raising kids? You don't even have any!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I've played a dad on TV. I know what I'm doing.

jokes.text: Are you still crying about your damn baby?
jokes.setup: Rachel mentions Emma being gone with what appears to be some emotional sadness; Monica has zero sympathy for this amid her wedding-planner stress
jokes.punchline: Monica snaps 'Are you still crying about your damn baby?' — framing Rachel's maternal emotion as an inconvenient nuisance
jokes.explanation: Monica's total tunnel vision on the wedding makes 'are you still crying about your damn baby?' land as a great character moment. The word 'damn' applied to a baby is a funny collision of registers. Concise and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's like being cut from the team. But instead of football, it's like being cut from... synchronized swimming.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No wait, rhythmic gymnastics.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ice dancing. I'm upset I'm not in the ice dancing.

jokes.text: You see these clowns all the time. You must give me the name of your wedding planner. I wanna throw a really tense party.
jokes.setup: Monica is barking orders at everyone and keeping people on a tight 20-second-per-person schedule; Mike's parents observe the chaos
jokes.punchline: An unidentified character (Mike's parents) sarcastically says they want Monica's wedding planner's number so they can 'throw a really tense party'
jokes.explanation: A sharp observational line about Monica's energy. 'A really tense party' is good writing — it's the specific, slightly odd word choice ('tense' instead of 'stressful' or 'uptight') that elevates it above a generic Monica-is-controlling joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm stuck watching women's volleyball again. Why does this keep happening to me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Football.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Football. You need football. Not women's sports, just... football.

jokes.text: On one hand, you're happy for them. On the other, it's hard to let go. / How do you want to divide up the holidays?
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to bond with Mike's parents as Phoebe's surrogate dad, saying something vaguely parental about children growing up
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately cuts to 'How do you want to divide up the holidays?' — treating a platitude about parental love as an opening negotiation with Mike's parents as if they're co-grandparents
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Joey is so completely committed to the father-figure role that he immediately jumps to divorced-co-parent logistics (holiday splitting) with people he just met. The jump from emotional platitude to practical negotiation is a classic misdirection structure. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You sent a fax?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, why? Don't you have a fax?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you should get one.

jokes.text: Who in God's name are you? / I'm not that fond of you either, buddy. I'm just trying to be nice for the kids.
jokes.setup: Mike's father has no idea who Joey is or why this stranger is discussing holiday plans with him
jokes.punchline: Joey, offended, responds 'I'm not that fond of you either, buddy' — which is absurd because (a) he doesn't know this man and (b) he initiated the conversation — then adds 'I'm just trying to be nice for the kids' as if they're in a custody battle
jokes.explanation: Joey's wounded 'I'm not that fond of you either, buddy' is the ideal escalation — he's offended by the confusion even though he's the one who created it. 'Just trying to be nice for the kids' perfectly completes the divorced-co-parent illusion he's constructed. The escalation from platitude to negotiation to mild hostility is well-paced comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? This is just a rehearsal.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A rehearsal for what?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: For being left out tomorrow.

jokes.text: I thought we'd be groomsmen. They would have asked us by now. / When did they ask you to be a bridesmaid? / November. / I wanna say it's not looking good.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler realize they haven't been asked to be in the wedding party and are sitting alone with nothing to do at the rehearsal dinner
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dawning realization is confirmed by Ross — bridesmaids were asked in November — leading to Chandler's perfectly understated 'I wanna say it's not looking good'
jokes.explanation: 'I wanna say it's not looking good' is a good Chandler-ism — the hedging 'I wanna say' before stating an obvious conclusion is a nice verbal tic. The beat works as setup for the Ross/Chandler exclusion subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hello, I'm Chandler Bing, and I will be your groomsman.

jokes.text: Well, this is really awkward. / Oh, and I can leave.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has to tell Ross and Chandler to their faces that they're not in the wedding; the moment becomes visibly painful and awkward
jokes.punchline: Mike, who has zero stake in this conflict, calmly offers 'Oh, and I can leave' — the groom offering to exit his own wedding party conversation
jokes.explanation: Mike's non-involvement in the friends' drama is a recurring source of gentle comedy, and his offer to leave his own wedding situation is a good beat. Very economical. Slightly underused as a character but functions well as a quick reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're going down.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Downer.

jokes.text: This is like figure skating team all over again. / I mean, synchronized swimming. / I mean-- I mean, the balance beam. / Help me. / Football. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Chandler is devastated about not being in the wedding and reaches for a sports analogy to express being cut from a team
jokes.punchline: He lists increasingly non-masculine sports (figure skating, synchronized swimming, balance beam) before Ross rescues him with 'football' — which Chandler gratefully accepts
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best comedic exchanges. The escalating list of increasingly 'unmanly' sports Chandler has apparently tried out for (figure skating → synchronized swimming → balance beam) builds perfectly, with 'Help me' as the pivot — a vulnerability that makes Ross's 'Football' rescue and Chandler's 'Thank you' land as a genuine comedic partnership moment. The structure is immaculate: escalation + distress signal + rescue + gratitude. Very Ross-and-Chandler-specific dynamic. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What do figure skaters say to each other for good luck?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wouldn't know. I didn't make the team.

jokes.text: Oh, Pheebs, spit that out. That has pork in it. / I thought the pot stickers were supposed to be vegetarian? / Yeah, I changed them. I sent you a fax about it. / I don't have a fax machine. / Well, then there are gonna be a few surprises.
jokes.setup: Monica has been changing menu items for Phoebe's (vegetarian) wedding without consulting her, communicating via fax
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't have a fax machine, making all of Monica's notifications void — Monica's response is the perfectly ominous 'Well, then there are gonna be a few surprises'
jokes.explanation: Monica using 'fax machine' as the bureaucratic shield for all her unauthorized wedding changes is funny on its own, but 'Well, then there are gonna be a few surprises' is the gem — it's simultaneously ominous, oblivious, and perfectly Monica. The implication that there are many more unauthorized changes (not just the pot stickers) is rich. Good structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. You're gonna marry Phoebe?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yes, that's right.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. So that's strike one.

jokes.text: Fine. We're sitting here, alone, doing nothing. It's our rehearsal for tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Ross and Chandler how it's going as they sit excluded from all the rehearsal dinner activity
jokes.punchline: Ross bitterly frames their doing-nothing as a 'rehearsal' for tomorrow — when they'll also be doing nothing at the actual wedding
jokes.explanation: A clever structural joke — the idea that their 'rehearsal' for the wedding is sitting around excluded parallels the rehearsal-dinner concept nicely. Ross's bitter deadpan is well-deployed here. Clean, economical, and gets a genuine laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could move in with Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, not really. Joey's apartment is too small.

jokes.text: What happened? / Who cares? And...?
jokes.setup: Mike tells them one of his groomsmen had an emergency and can't make it; Ross asks what happened out of genuine concern
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately cuts off any sympathy with 'Who cares? And...?' — skipping the niceties to get to whether one of them gets the spot
jokes.explanation: Chandler's 'Who cares? And...?' is excellent economy — two words dismiss an entire line of inquiry and pivot to what they actually care about. It also characterizes Chandler's slightly selfish side under social pressure. The 'And...?' trailing off is a great comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Strike three, you're out!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Come on, give me another chance.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. But this is it. One more strike and you're... out of the game for like twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Pick me. I look great in a tux, and I won't steal focus.
jokes.setup: Mike says there's only room for one groomsman, and both Ross and Chandler eagerly volunteer; they begin making their cases
jokes.punchline: Ross's campaign promise that he 'won't steal focus' is immediately undercut by the fact that saying it is itself a form of focus-stealing
jokes.explanation: A decent setup for the Ross/Chandler competition. The 'I won't steal focus' claim has light ironic undertone but the joke doesn't fully develop its own contradiction — the script doesn't call it out. Functional but not punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I would say we love you too, but let's be honest - you're kind of a lot to handle.

jokes.text: Well, if Phoebe's choosing, then say hello to Mike's next groomsman. / Oh, I will. But I will need a mirror, as he is me. / Please. You're going down. / You are going 'downer.'
jokes.setup: Mike passes the choice to Phoebe; Ross and Chandler immediately begin trash-talking each other
jokes.punchline: Chandler tries to one-up Ross's 'you're going down' with 'you are going downer' — a deliberately weak, grammatically mangled comeback that works because it's so bad
jokes.explanation: 'You are going downer' is a great Chandler joke because it's intentionally a terrible comeback — Chandler is so competitive he reaches for the trash-talk but can't quite execute it. The deliberate badness is the point, which is a clever self-aware move by the writers.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Get in, do your thing, and get out.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's what she said.

jokes.text: They say that on the figure skating team? / I wouldn't know. I didn't make it.
jokes.setup: Ross mocks Chandler's weak trash-talk by asking if that's what they say on the figure skating team
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'I wouldn't know. I didn't make it.' — which both maintains the fiction of the figure skating team and loops back to the original joke about being cut from teams
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback. The earlier joke established Chandler tried out for multiple teams and failed; this callback deepens it by having Chandler simultaneously mock-defend the figure skating team (maintaining the fiction) while also admitting he didn't make it. 'I wouldn't know. I didn't make it.' is beautifully timed and economical. The double layer — callback + self-deprecation — earns close to an 8.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Mary Ellen couldn't be here tonight, and I'm not gonna get into why.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She's in rehab.

jokes.text: So, what are your intentions with my Phoebe? / I intend to marry her. / Oh, a wiseacre.
jokes.setup: Joey, in full surrogate-dad mode, confronts Mike with the classic father-of-the-bride question about his intentions
jokes.punchline: Mike answers literally and correctly ('I intend to marry her') and Joey, expecting vague declarations of love, dismisses him as 'a wiseacre' — as if being direct is cheating
jokes.explanation: Mike's literal answer to a rhetorical question is a classic misdirection — the cliché father-of-the-bride scene expects a heartfelt response, and 'I intend to marry her' (which is technically perfect) earns Joey's indignation. 'A wiseacre' is a great word for Joey to use — slightly old-fashioned, very 'concerned father.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm firing you as my maid of honor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Cheers!

jokes.text: Isn't that kind of unstable? / No more so than acting. / Strike two.
jokes.setup: Joey questions whether a musician can stably support Phoebe; Mike notes that acting (Joey's career) is equally unstable
jokes.punchline: Mike's perfectly logical 'No more so than acting' — pointing out Joey's hypocrisy — earns 'Strike two,' with Joey refusing to acknowledge the point
jokes.explanation: Mike's comeback is logically airtight and character-specific (he's identifying Joey's blind spot), and Joey's refusal to concede the point ('Strike two') is perfectly Joey — he doesn't process the hypocrisy at all. The 'strikes' system Joey has imposed is itself funny. Good character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I would eat those.

jokes.text: You're right. She probably will support me. Hey, unless we move in with you, Dad.
jokes.setup: Mike has already conceded Phoebe might support him; he now needles Joey further by suggesting they move in with 'Dad'
jokes.punchline: 'Hey, unless we move in with you, Dad' — Mike weaponizes Joey's self-imposed father role against him, earning a 'Strike three'
jokes.explanation: Mike has found the right way to get under Joey's skin — using the dad fiction Joey created against him. 'Unless we move in with you, Dad' is a clever reversal. The escalating strikes system (strike two → strike three) also gives the scene good comic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I won these awards for my organizational skills. See? 'Best Closet Organization 1997,' 'Most Color-Coordinated Linen Closet 1998,' 'Bathroom Cabinet Excellence 1999.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, didn't you make those yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but that doesn't make them any less valid!

jokes.text: That Mike has got no respect. I'm not sure about him. / Wait, that's not him. There he is.
jokes.setup: Joey reports to someone that he's 'not sure about' Mike after the confrontational conversation; then we realize he was looking at the wrong person entirely
jokes.punchline: 'Wait, that's not him. There he is.' — Joey has been judging a random stranger instead of Mike, undercutting his whole alpha-dad posture
jokes.explanation: A quick visual gag that works as a puncture of Joey's tough-dad posturing. The reveal that he was glaring at the wrong man simultaneously makes him look foolish and sweetly harmless. Good economy; the beat is over in two lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, I need to talk to you about something important. Monica asked me to be a groomsman and I was thinking—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I... um... you look... that dress is...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? What were you saying?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: Just not enough to put us in the original wedding party. / Such bitterness. / Best to keep that attitude in the seats.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Ross and Chandler she loves them both; Chandler or Ross immediately adds the biting qualifier about not being in the wedding party
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'Such bitterness. Best to keep that attitude in the seats' — dismissing their grievance while confirming they will indeed be sitting
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's 'Best to keep that attitude in the seats' is a nicely acidic comeback — she acknowledges the bitterness and redirects it without apologizing. Good economy in the line.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, come on. Think about it. I'm a paleontologist, I have a steady job, I'm stable, I'm reliable—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I have a job too!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, but you're not me. I'm offering you security, a future—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you're great, but you've been in love with me since high school. That's not stability, that's obsession. And Chandler? He makes me laugh, but he can't commit to anything except sarcasm. So really, I'm choosing neither of you and going to Paris.

jokes.text: Listen, I have a very special bridesmaid task for you to do. / Goody! What is it? / Well, there's a spot open for only one groomsman, and you have to choose between Ross and Chandler. So good luck with that.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Rachel she has a 'very special bridesmaid task,' building Rachel's (and the audience's) expectation of something glamorous or meaningful
jokes.punchline: The special task is choosing between Ross and Chandler for the groomsman spot — essentially offloading an impossible social problem onto Rachel
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — she frames the impossible task as a gift and walks away. 'So good luck with that' is the perfect Phoebe exit line: cheerful, oblivious to the cruelty, and followed by immediate departure. The structure (misdirection of 'special task' + comedic anti-climax) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I love you! You're like a genius! You just... you just made up a word and it means something! That's incredible!

jokes.text: I guess I have to find a new bridesmaid. / I'll do it!
jokes.setup: Rachel is resisting being the one to choose between Ross and Chandler; Phoebe threatens to find a new bridesmaid
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately folds and agrees to do it — Phoebe's social leverage works instantly
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional button on the previous joke. Rachel's immediate capitulation is funny but predictable — the 'I'll do it!' reversal is telegraphed. Works as a beat but isn't a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm borrowing lines from a bad audition I had. The guy doing the fake Italian accent was terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're using his bad accent?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm using his lines! The accent just... came with them.

jokes.text: It's 2100 hours. / Do I have time to go to the bathroom? / You had a bathroom break at 2030. Pee on your own time, Mike.
jokes.setup: Monica is running the rehearsal dinner like a military operation with strict time management
jokes.punchline: Monica has tracked Mike's bathroom break schedule and denies him bathroom time — 'Pee on your own time, Mike' — treating biological needs as an inefficiency
jokes.explanation: 'Pee on your own time, Mike' is a genuinely great line — the word 'pee' in what is otherwise a hyper-formal military-speak monologue creates a tonal collision that works perfectly. Monica telling the groom when he can urinate is a peak Monica-as-control-freak moment. High quotability; this line would get repeated.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: That was a lousy movie.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That wasn't the movie. That was me talking about my family.

jokes.text: You just get in, do your thing, and get out. / Is that what you say to Chandler?
jokes.setup: Monica is giving wedding toast advice: 'get in, do your thing, get out'
jokes.punchline: Joey's interpretation of 'get in, do your thing, get out' as a description of Monica and Chandler's sex life — delivered as a casual aside
jokes.explanation: A classic double entendre setup. Monica's toast instructions ('get in, do your thing, get out') are an accidental sex metaphor and Joey's callback is perfectly timed. The joke is predictable — the audience sees it coming — but the execution is clean and Monica's frosty '2101 and I am not amused' response is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was picked last in gym class. Behind a foreign exchange student who didn't even know what baseball was.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The teacher had to explain to him that you hit the ball with the bat. He thought I was volunteering for some kind of punishment.

jokes.text: It's 2101, and I am not amused.
jokes.setup: Joey has just made a sex joke at Monica's expense
jokes.punchline: Monica's response specifies the exact military time (2101 — one minute after her last timestamp) and states she is 'not amused' in a mock-regal manner
jokes.explanation: The fact that Monica gives the exact time (2101) rather than just saying 'right now' is the detail that elevates this. 'I am not amused' is Victorian in register — Monica as tiny, furious queen. The timestamp specificity makes it a callback to her military persona and a great character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm a groomsman! Finally, someone had to make room for me!

jokes.text: Oh, okay. I thought about it, and I fixed him up with my friend Mary Ellen, who couldn't be here tonight, because... It's not important. Well, she's in rehab.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is giving a toast explaining how she and Mike met through Joey setting them up
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually mentions her friend Mary Ellen is 'in rehab' after initially saying 'it's not important' — a perfect Phoebe overshare with a dark twist
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe overshare structure: start with a dismissal ('it's not important'), then immediately share the thing anyway ('she's in rehab'). The setup-within-the-setup is tight. It's also dark in a Phoebe-specific way — her social circle includes people in rehab and in prison and she treats both with equal breezy nonchalance. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why is there a giant ice sculpture in the hallway?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's for the party tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man, I have the weirdest impulse right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I want to lick it like a flagpole.

jokes.text: Joey said that he was fixing me up with his friend Mike — only he didn't have a friend Mike, so he just brought my Mike.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is recounting how she met Mike; Joey had promised to set her up with 'his friend Mike'
jokes.punchline: Joey didn't actually have a friend named Mike — he found a random Mike and brought him — which is both absurd and completely in character
jokes.explanation: This joke rewards fans of the show's history (the Phoebe/Mike setup episode in season 9). Joey's solution to not knowing a Mike — just finding one — is completely consistent with his character and lands as both ridiculous and weirdly sweet. The fact that it worked out is the romantic kicker the show leans into.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Why don't you guys just make my dog the groomsman?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Your dog?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's great at standing around and not saying anything stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey!

jokes.text: I wanna take a moment to mention my mother, who couldn't be here. / Oh, God. / And... moment's over.
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions her deceased mother in the middle of her rambling toast; the audience (characters) braces for a heavy moment
jokes.punchline: 'Moment's over' — Phoebe dispenses with the grief beat in approximately two seconds
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and very high on quotability. The structure is perfect: Phoebe calls for a solemn moment of remembrance, an unseen character (or collective) reacts with 'Oh, God' anticipating a lengthy emotional detour, and then Phoebe's 'moment's over' comes almost immediately. The joke is in the gap between the gravity of losing a mother and Phoebe's breezy speed of processing it. Economy is nearly perfect — the punchline is two words. Very Phoebe-specific. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I pick the dog.

jokes.text: Oh, but you need to know that to get that. / So... Oh, well, okay. / I... Okay.
jokes.setup: Phoebe's toast is spiraling into a chaotic, incoherent stream of consciousness — she's clearly lost the thread
jokes.punchline: The toast becomes an extended cringe sequence of Phoebe talking herself into dead ends, with 'I... Okay.' as a helpless acknowledgment that she's lost
jokes.explanation: The rambling toast is funny as a character bit but the humor is diffuse across several lines rather than concentrated in a single punchline. This scores lower than the 'moment's over' joke because it's sustained cringe that works on stage but doesn't have a sharp comedic payoff — it sets up the Monica firing moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Monica, I'm so overwhelmed. Can you please help me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Of course! What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I need you to be controlling again.

jokes.text: Monica, I can't do it like this! / ...I just wanted a simple wedding where my fiancé can go to the bathroom any time he wants!
jokes.setup: Phoebe finally snaps at Monica's excessive control of the wedding, listing her grievances
jokes.punchline: Among her list of demands, 'my fiancé can go to the bathroom any time he wants' — a callback to Monica's earlier military-time bathroom-scheduling incident
jokes.explanation: The bathroom callback is effective because it's specific — not just 'I want a normal wedding' but 'my fiancé should be allowed to pee.' The specificity makes it funnier than a generic complaint. It also gives the episode's Monica-as-military-planner running gag a satisfying payoff before the firing scene.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: When did you start watching the news?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Since I found out the weather girl is hot.

jokes.text: You know what? You're done. / What? / You're fired!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has reached her breaking point with Monica's control over the wedding
jokes.punchline: Phoebe fires Monica — the bride fires her wedding planner/best friend — delivered with crisp decisiveness
jokes.explanation: The firing works as a comedic beat and a plot pivot. 'You're done. What? You're fired!' is well-structured with the 'What?' giving Monica a beat to be confused before the full declaration. Phoebe firing her best friend is funny but also sets up the later plot of Monica being re-hired.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: My mom seems unusually pleased with the street wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I may have put something in her coffee this morning.

jokes.text: Joey, listen, this is gonna be bridesmaid central. I had to move a couple things in the fridge to make room for the corsages. / Man! I wouldn't have had breakfast if I knew there was gonna be corsages.
jokes.setup: Rachel explains the apartment logistics — corsages are in the fridge where food was
jokes.punchline: Joey's devastation that the corsages displaced his food — 'I wouldn't have had breakfast' — reveals he ate only because the food was there, not because he was hungry
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey-and-food joke. The logic is impeccable Joey logic: he's not sad the food is gone, he's sad he could have saved it by not eating it. 'I wouldn't have had breakfast' as an expression of regret over corsage placement is very character-specific. High character integration for Joey's food obsession.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I can do this. It's just a small dog. How bad could it be?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! Oh my God! It's a vicious beast! It's trying to kill me!

jokes.text: What about in high school when that yogurt store let you go for sampling toppings? / Everyone there did that. / Yeah, but did everybody owe 3 grand at the end of the summer?
jokes.setup: Monica objects to being called 'fired,' saying she's never been fired before; Rachel (or someone) brings up the yogurt store
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'sampling toppings' to owing 3 thousand dollars in topping debt by end of summer — an absurd and very specific detail about the depth of Monica's topping addiction
jokes.explanation: The yogurt store detail is excellent comedy writing: 'sampling toppings' is innocuous, but '$3,000 in debt by end of summer' implies Monica was essentially a topping-addict who ran a tab. The specificity of '$3 grand' and 'end of summer' makes it feel like a real, detailed history rather than a throwaway joke. Very Monica-specific — her food obsession plus her financial precision are both embedded in the gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm still ordained.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, it's great for getting discounts on the subway.

jokes.text: I have won awards for my organizational skills. / You've won awards? / I printed them out on my computer.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to convince Phoebe she's the right person to handle the wedding logistics, citing awards
jokes.punchline: The 'awards' were self-generated — Monica printed out her own certificates on her computer
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. Monica printing out her own organizational awards is so true to her character — her obsessive need for external validation, her competence paired with insecurity, her inability to recognize the irony — that it functions as a perfect character-comedy gem. 'I printed them out on my computer' is delivered as if this is a completely normal thing to do. High quotability and high character integration. Close to a 9 on craft because it's so specifically Monica and so perfectly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Do ministers really ride the subway for free?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I looked into it. It's a biblical loophole.

jokes.text: This wedding isn't about you. / It's not? Then who's it about? / Well, it used to be about me, but now I have no idea.
jokes.setup: Monica corrects Ross/Chandler that the wedding isn't about them; someone (Phoebe?) turns it back on Monica
jokes.punchline: Monica's admission that the wedding 'used to be about me' — perfectly capturing how Monica's control-freak nature made it her event — followed by 'now I have no idea' after being fired
jokes.explanation: Monica saying the wedding 'used to be about me' is a great self-aware moment — she's not correcting herself, she's genuinely confused about who it's for now. 'Now I have no idea' is sad-funny. Good character integration for the Monica subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I want you to wear the headset in bed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, we have sex on Thursdays at 8 PM. That's it. I have a whole schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You scheduled sex?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes. Thursday, 20:00 hours. It's very efficient.

jokes.text: If I said yes, that would freak you out, wouldn't it?
jokes.setup: Ross is making his case to Rachel to be chosen as groomsman, rattling off their shared history (went out, have a child together); he asks 'Do you and Chandler have a child together?'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response — 'If I said yes, that would freak you out, wouldn't it?' — implies she might be entertaining the idea of saying yes, turning Ross's rhetorical question back on him with a mild threat
jokes.explanation: A quick Rachel-as-troublemaker beat. The joke is in Rachel briefly making Ross think she might confirm it. Good economy but a fairly predictable 'what if I said yes?' reversal. It's funny in the context of Rachel and Ross's history but doesn't have the originality for a higher score.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not me, it's the dog.

jokes.text: If you pick Chandler, he's gonna be whispering stupid jokes in your ear the whole time.
jokes.setup: Ross is making his final case to Rachel why she should choose him over Chandler
jokes.punchline: Ross attacking Chandler for 'whispering stupid jokes' is itself a form of manipulative lobbying — the slight hypocrisy of Ross making a case by badmouthing Chandler
jokes.explanation: Functional plot dialogue with mild character comedy. The joke is Ross trying to make Rachel laugh while simultaneously warning her Chandler will make her laugh. It's a bit circular and doesn't fully land as a sharp joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm freezing in this dress.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My blue skin from the cold will be my 'something blue.'

jokes.text: Oh, you are the lesser of two evils. / Yes!
jokes.setup: Rachel has finally decided who to pick for groomsman
jokes.punchline: She tells Ross he's the 'lesser of two evils' — the most backhanded possible compliment — and Ross's jubilant 'Yes!' shows he will take any win
jokes.explanation: Ross's enthusiasm at being called 'the lesser of two evils' perfectly encapsulates his desperation for inclusion. The juxtaposition of Rachel's dismissive phrasing and Ross's celebration of it is a small but sharp character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's so cold out here, I can't feel my... you know.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm sure it's still there, but I can't feel it.

jokes.text: I cannot believe you played the Emma card. / Oh, please. I was prepared to offer you my body. / Oh, my God! And I didn't hold out.
jokes.setup: Rachel accuses Ross of using their daughter Emma as leverage to get picked; Ross reveals he had an even more extreme card ready
jokes.punchline: Ross was prepared to offer Rachel his body — she realizes she could have gotten more than a groomsman spot and is appalled she didn't hold out
jokes.explanation: Rachel's 'And I didn't hold out' as a response to learning she could have gotten sexual favors is a great line — the regret is genuine and funny. The joke rewards the Ross/Rachel history (the audience knows this dynamic) and the structure escalates from emotional manipulation (the Emma card) to physical (his body) in a way that works both as dark comedy and as Ross/Rachel relationship humor.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it me, or is it freezing in here?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's freezing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I think the dog might be dying.

jokes.text: You know, normally, that would hurt my feelings, but today, I'm a groomsman.
jokes.setup: Rachel's 'and I didn't hold out' implicitly insults Ross's desirability; Ross acknowledges it normally would sting
jokes.punchline: Ross's groomsman joy completely overrides any self-esteem concerns — 'but today, I'm a groomsman' — the win matters more than the insult
jokes.explanation: A good button on the exchange. Ross's pride in being a groomsman is hilariously out of proportion, and his gracious acceptance of the insult-because-groomsman is an affectionate character moment. The rhythm of 'normally, that would hurt my feelings, but today...' is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that was so beautiful. I'm so happy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you're married!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! And now I have to change my name on all my credit cards. Do you know how many identities I have?

jokes.text: 'Lorkins'? What the hell are 'lorkins'? / Mike, if you were Swedish and you were saying the word 'lorkins,' what flower would that be? / Orchids? / Right there! That's why I'm marrying you.
jokes.setup: Monica is on the phone with 'Sven' (a Swedish florist) trying to understand what flower he's describing; the word 'lorkins' is incomprehensible to her
jokes.punchline: She asks her Swedish fiancé Mike to translate on the spot; he immediately gets it ('Orchids?'); Phoebe's 'That's why I'm marrying you' is a romantic beat that's also a joke about how low the bar is
jokes.explanation: A charming bit. 'Lorkins' is a great made-up word that sounds Swedish-ish, the problem-solving is funny (asking your Swedish fiancé to translate an improvised word), and 'That's why I'm marrying you' as the punchline works on two levels — romantic and absurdist (she's marrying him because he's a Swedish-to-English translator in a pinch). Good originality.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going home at 2300 hours.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, it's 11 PM. Just say 11 PM.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I have a very specific schedule. Chandler and I have intimacy blocked out from 11:15 to 11:27.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: 12 minutes? That includes the cuddling?

jokes.text: Are you rehearsing for some really bad Mafia movie? / More back talk. And yes, I may be borrowing a few lines from my recent unsuccessful audition for Family Honor 2: This A-Time It's A-Personal.
jokes.setup: Joey has been doing an over-the-top Godfather-style intimidation scene with Mike, complete with dramatic pauses and power positioning
jokes.punchline: Joey admits he's recycling lines from a failed Mafia movie audition — 'Family Honor 2: This A-Time It's A-Personal' — the title being a mangled mock-sequel title that's perfect in its badness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuinely exceptional jokes. 'Family Honor 2: This A-Time It's A-Personal' is a masterwork of fake bad movie title comedy — 'This A-Time' is the perfect Italian-accented mangling of 'This Time,' the sequel structure is exactly the kind of bad sequel title that actually exists, and the fact that Joey LOST this audition implies the movie went with someone doing it even worse. The character integration is near-perfect (Joey recycling failed audition material as real-life dialogue is very Joey). The title alone is quotable and distinctive. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, boy. Come on. Do your business. Please? Please do your business.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm begging you. Just go to the bathroom. Any bathroom. Yours!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Please, I'm missing my own wedding!

jokes.text: That must have been one lousy movie. / That was me!
jokes.setup: Joey has just delivered a sincere, earnest speech about family and protecting Phoebe ('there's nothing more important in the whole world than family')
jokes.punchline: Mike's 'That must have been one lousy movie' — assuming the heartfelt speech was also borrowed from the Mafia film — and Joey's wounded 'That was me!' defending his genuine emotion
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback and subversion. The structure is perfect: Joey's sincere declaration of love for Phoebe and family sounds exactly like his Mafia movie dialogue, so Mike naturally assumes it's recycled. Joey's wounded 'That was me!' is a great punchline because it's both a correction and an accidental self-commentary — the audience realizes the Mafia movie and Joey's real feelings are indistinguishable. Economy is excellent; the whole exchange is two lines. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: If you choose me, you'll be getting some comedy. / Even so... I think I'm gonna pick Ross.
jokes.setup: Chandler makes his final pitch to Rachel, promising 'comedy' as his value proposition for being a groomsman
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'Even so... I think I'm gonna pick Ross' — she acknowledges the comedy offer but still picks Ross, which is a mild burn on Chandler's pitch
jokes.explanation: A quick, mild joke that works more as plot progression than as a standout comedic moment. 'Even so' is a funny dismissal of Chandler's comedy pitch, but the joke doesn't have strong originality.

jokes.text: See, when I was a kid, I was always left out of everything... I was always picked last in gym, even behind that fat exchange student who didn't know the rules to baseball. This guy would strike out and then run to third.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to emotionally manipulate Rachel into choosing him by telling a sob story about being picked last in gym
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 'the fat exchange student who didn't know the rules of baseball' — who would 'strike out and then run to third' — is so specific and vivid it becomes its own comedic world
jokes.explanation: The details make this joke work: 'struck out and then ran to third' is a perfect detail — it's specific, visual, and tells you everything about the student's total incomprehension of baseball. It also retroactively confirms that even that person was chosen before Chandler, which is devastating-funny. Good storytelling economy.

jokes.text: All right, fine, I pick you. / Yes! / Make 'groom' for Chandler.
jokes.setup: Rachel finally gives in to Chandler's emotional manipulation and picks him; Chandler celebrates
jokes.punchline: Chandler's victory cheer is 'Make groom for Chandler' — a pun on 'make room' and 'groomsman'
jokes.explanation: 'Make groom for Chandler' is a decent pun (groom/room) in the classic Chandler wordplay tradition. It's not a surprising or particularly sharp joke but it's well-deployed as a celebration moment and consistent with Chandler's character voice.

jokes.text: And thanks for all the wedding night advice. That didn't make me uncomfortable at all.
jokes.setup: Monica has apparently been getting unsolicited wedding night (sex) advice from the Reverend during her planning call
jokes.punchline: 'That didn't make me uncomfortable at all' — delivered in Monica's dry sarcastic voice, implying she was deeply uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: A quick off-the-top joke about the Reverend being inappropriately chatty about the wedding night. Monica's deadpan sarcasm works but the joke is fairly generic — the idea of a minister giving sex advice isn't fresh territory.

jokes.text: Did you guys know that there's a giant ice sculpture in the hall? / Oh, my God, what's it doing here? / I guess it got sent to the billing address as opposed to the shipping address. / What a pickle.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the wedding day chaos, a massive ice sculpture has been delivered to the wrong location — the apartment building instead of the wedding venue
jokes.punchline: Chandler's bureaucratic 'billing address vs. shipping address' explanation, followed by his laconic 'What a pickle' — treating a catastrophic wedding logistics failure as a minor clerical issue
jokes.explanation: 'What a pickle' as Chandler's response to wedding catastrophe is very Chandler — the calm, slightly archaic phrase ('pickle') in the face of disaster. The billing/shipping address explanation is bureaucratic comedy that works for his character. Also seeds the ice sculpture gag that pays off later.

jokes.text: How bad do you wanna stick your tongue on that?
jokes.setup: Monica is panicking about everything going wrong (club lost power, giant ice sculpture in the hall, blizzard coming)
jokes.punchline: Chandler, amid Monica's breakdown, randomly asks if anyone wants to lick the ice sculpture — a completely non-sequitur childish impulse
jokes.explanation: Chandler's total tonal pivot — from Monica's crisis to 'how bad do you wanna stick your tongue on that?' — is a great comedic beat. The question is specific (tongue, not just touch), which makes it funnier. It's also a universal impulse that any audience can relate to, which gives it strong observational comedy energy. The economy is perfect.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. I know why I'm being such an ass. Why are you?
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are both hanging around being weird/difficult about the groomsman situation; Chandler asks what's going on
jokes.punchline: Ross's self-aware 'I know why I'm being such an ass' — followed by turning it on Chandler — is a great beat because Ross doesn't often acknowledge his own behavior
jokes.explanation: Ross calling himself an ass is funny because it's unusually self-aware for him, and immediately redirecting it at Chandler ('Why are you?') keeps both characters in the joke. The structure — partial self-awareness that immediately becomes an accusation — is clever.

jokes.text: Did Rachel say you could be in the wedding? / Yes. / She told me that too! / I don't believe this. I played the Emma card. / I looked into my soul.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler discover Rachel told both of them they'd be the groomsman
jokes.punchline: Their parallel complaints: Ross played the Emma card (using his daughter as leverage) and Chandler 'looked into his soul' (vulnerable emotional manipulation) — both revealed as equally cynical strategies
jokes.explanation: The parallel confessions are well-structured: each man reveals his manipulation tactic, and the juxtaposition ('I played the Emma card' vs. 'I looked into my soul') perfectly captures the difference between Ross (uses external props — his baby) and Chandler (goes internal but equally cynically). Both callbacks land simultaneously and reward attentive viewers. 'I looked into my soul' is a great Chandler line — it sounds profound but was entirely strategic.

jokes.text: In my defense, you weren't supposed to tell each other!
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler confront Rachel about telling them both they'd be the groomsman
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'defense' is entirely about how the deception should have remained undiscovered — she's not apologizing for lying, just for being found out
jokes.explanation: Classic Rachel defense: her only regret is operational failure, not the lie itself. 'You weren't supposed to tell each other!' is a great line — it's both deeply self-serving and weirdly logical within Rachel's worldview. The audience immediately recognizes this as very Rachel.

jokes.text: Rach, Rach? Knock-knock. / Who's there? / I'll tell you at the wedding.
jokes.setup: Ross is being competitive about the groomsman role and trying to demonstrate his joke-making abilities to Rachel to prove he's fun
jokes.punchline: 'I'll tell you at the wedding' — Ross doesn't have a punchline but promises to deliver one at the ceremony, essentially making a reservation for a future joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most original jokes. The knock-knock joke structure is familiar but the subversion — having no punchline and promising to deliver it at the wedding — is a fresh meta-twist. It works on multiple levels: it's absurd (a deferred knock-knock joke), character-specific (Ross is so desperate he's using a placeholder joke), and briefly meta (a joke about promising to tell a joke later). The punchline IS that there's no punchline. Very high economy and originality. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Oh, you haven't picked yet? Oh, good, because I had an idea. I thought it would be fun if the third groomsman was my family dog, Chappy.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are pressuring Rachel to finally make a decision; Mike walks in unaware of the drama
jokes.punchline: Mike casually suggests his family dog, Chappy, as the third groomsman — entering the conversation with a completely different and absurd solution
jokes.explanation: Mike's dog-as-groomsman suggestion is a good absurdist pivot that immediately resolves the Ross/Chandler standoff in the most ridiculous way. It also plants Chappy, who becomes important later. The nonchalance of Mike's delivery ('I thought it would be fun') is key.

jokes.text: Wow, this is a tough one. I think I'm gonna have to go with the dog.
jokes.setup: Rachel is asked to choose between Ross, Chandler, and now a dog named Chappy for the groomsman role
jokes.punchline: Rachel pretends to deliberate seriously before choosing the dog — the ultimate burn on both Ross and Chandler
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna have to go with the dog' is a great punchline — Rachel's faux-serious deliberation followed by picking Chappy is both a character moment (Rachel being delightfully petty) and a funny resolution to the whole groomsman subplot. The fact that the dog beats both Ross and Chandler is the comedic peak of that plotline.

jokes.text: Help me. / What? / I want you to be crazy bitch again.
jokes.setup: Everything is falling apart — the chef is at the wrong venue, food and drinks are separated from their staff. Phoebe begs Monica for help.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explicitly asks Monica to 'be crazy bitch again' — requesting the exact controlling behavior she fired Monica for earlier
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable lines. 'I want you to be crazy bitch again' is structurally perfect — it's the callback to Monica being fired, it's an honest acknowledgment of what Monica's controlling behavior actually is, and Phoebe saying it with desperate sincerity is hilariously on-brand for both characters. The word 'again' is crucial — it confirms this is Monica's normal state. Very high quotability; this is a clip-worthy moment. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Oh, God, I have missed you so much.
jokes.setup: Monica has been given the headset back and invited to resume control
jokes.punchline: Monica says she's 'missed you so much' — to the headset, treating the return of her power and control like a reunion with a loved one
jokes.explanation: Monica saying 'I have missed you so much' to her headset (or her role as planner) is a great character beat. It's simultaneously sad and funny — this is the most intimate Monica has been all episode and it's directed at an earpiece. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: It's the worst snowstorm in 20 years. They already closed all the bridges and tunnels. But the band and the photographer are coming in from New Jersey. / I don't think they are.
jokes.setup: Ross delivers the snowstorm news, inadvertently noting that the out-of-town vendors (band, photographer) are coming from New Jersey — which is across a closed bridge
jokes.punchline: Chandler's perfectly understated 'I don't think they are' — not an expression of panic but a calm, logical observation
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deadpan is excellent — five words to deflate the disaster announcement. The humor is entirely in the understatement and the contrast with the chaos around him. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Looks like you're not gonna be in the wedding, either.
jokes.setup: Chandler is processing that the blizzard/closed bridges mean everything is off; he turns to Ross
jokes.punchline: Even in wedding-collapse chaos, Chandler's first instinct is to note that Ross is also now excluded — connecting the disaster back to their personal exclusion subplot
jokes.explanation: A quick, mean joke that works because Chandler's priorities (even amid a wedding crisis) are still the groomsman drama. It's the right beat to maintain the subplot through the blizzard crisis.

jokes.text: Since when do you watch the news? / For your information, since they hired a very hot weather girl.
jokes.setup: Joey just delivered weather/news information, which surprises Chandler since Joey doesn't watch the news
jokes.punchline: Joey has been watching the news specifically because of a 'very hot weather girl' — his civic engagement is entirely aesthetic
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey joke — his engagement with the world is filtered through attraction. 'A very hot weather girl' as Joey's reason for suddenly caring about news is entirely in character. The structure is straightforward but reliable.

jokes.text: Affirmative!
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike decide to get married on the street in the snow; Mike asks Monica if they can pull it off
jokes.punchline: Monica's single-word 'Affirmative!' — military-speak for 'yes' — perfectly encapsulates her whole character arc in the episode and signals she's fully back in power
jokes.explanation: One word. 'Affirmative!' is the culmination of Monica's military-planner persona that has run through the whole episode. It's not just funny in context — it also signals Monica is fully re-empowered, closes the Monica subplot, and does it with perfect economy (one word). Character integration is as high as it gets. The running gag earns its payoff here.

jokes.text: Okay, who left the ice sculpture on the steam grate?
jokes.setup: The ice sculpture was delivered to the wrong location; now it's outside on a steam grate
jokes.punchline: The ice sculpture — Monica's symbol of over-the-top wedding planning — is literally melting on a steam grate, visually and thematically collapsing the elaborate original plan
jokes.explanation: The ice sculpture on the steam grate is a good visual callback — it completes the story of the ice sculpture (delivered wrong → now melting) in a visually funny way. Monica's framing it as a who-did-it question is funny because someone clearly just set it down without thinking. Good running gag payoff.

jokes.text: I crushed a pill and put it in her drink.
jokes.setup: Mike's mother has just said she 'could look at the snow forever' — apparently calm and accepting of the street wedding setting
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually reveals he drugged her — 'I crushed a pill and put it in her drink' — explaining her serene acceptance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's darkest and funniest jokes. The setup is a sweet moment — Mike's mother peacefully accepting the imperfect wedding — and Chandler's reveal that she's medicated is a perfect dark subversion. 'I crushed a pill and put it in her drink' is delivered so casually that it takes a beat to process the full implication. High originality (you don't expect a drug-the-mother-in-law joke in a romantic wedding episode), great economy, very dark. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: You know, Chappy's too small to handle all this snow. Someone has to walk him down the aisle. / Would this person be in the wedding? / I guess. / I'll do it! / I'll do it!
jokes.setup: Chappy the dog (Mike's family dog/original groomsman) needs someone to walk him down the aisle because he's too small for the snow
jokes.punchline: Ross and Chandler immediately volunteer, their groomsman desperation instantly reignited by this new opening
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the groomsman rivalry. The pivot of 'would this person be in the wedding?' — confirming the stakes — and the immediate simultaneous 'I'll do it!' from both men is a good comedic beat. The fact that they're competing to walk a dog down the aisle is the right absurdist endpoint for the subplot.

jokes.text: Chandler, hello? I mean, aren't you scared of dogs? / I'm not scared. I'll just take little Chappy and-- / He can sense my fear! My throat is exposed!
jokes.setup: Ross points out Chandler is scared of dogs as a tactical counter-argument; Chandler dismisses this
jokes.punchline: Chappy immediately senses Chandler's fear and apparently lunges at his throat — 'He can sense my fear! My throat is exposed!' — confirming the dog phobia instantly
jokes.explanation: 'He can sense my fear! My throat is exposed!' is a great physical comedy line that works even in transcript form. The specificity of 'my throat is exposed' is the detail that makes it funny — Chandler's fear has fully taken over and he's framing the dog as a predator hunting a vital artery. Very quotable. The escalation from 'I'm not scared' to immediate throat-exposure panic is well-structured.

jokes.text: Hey, don't worry. I'm still ordained from your wedding. / Really? / Yeah. You think I'd give up being a minister and pay to ride the subway?
jokes.setup: The minister is snowed in and can't make it; Joey offers to perform the ceremony because he's still ordained from Monica and Chandler's wedding
jokes.punchline: 'You think I'd give up being a minister and pay to ride the subway?' — revealing Joey has been using his ministerial status to get free subway rides
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a gem of character comedy. The reveal that Joey has maintained his ordination specifically to avoid subway fare is perfect Joey — it's selfish, oblivious, and completely plausible. 'You think I'd give up being a minister' implies he's weighed the spiritual responsibility and found 'free subway rides' to be the decisive factor. High character integration, great originality, strong economy. The joke also has a lovely absurdist layer: does the subway actually honor ministerial status? Joey seems to think so. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Ministers don't ride the subway for free. / I had to read the Bible pretty carefully, but yeah, we do.
jokes.setup: Chandler (correctly) states that ministers don't get free subway rides
jokes.punchline: Joey insists they do — and that he found this in the Bible after careful reading — implying he read the entire Bible specifically to find the subway loophole
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'I had to read the Bible pretty carefully, but yeah, we do' is extraordinary for several reasons: (1) It implies Joey read the entire Bible with his primary motivation being subway loophole detection; (2) 'pretty carefully' suggests the subway clause is obscure, requiring study; (3) Joey's confidence ('yeah, we do') shows he's fully convinced he's right; (4) it's simultaneously absurd, character-specific, and logically consistent within Joey's worldview. This is the episode's closest moment to genuine classic sitcom comedy writing. High quotability, near-perfect character integration, and the right level of absurdism. Clear standout.

jokes.text: Okay, Joey's doing the ceremony, and Chandler's giving you away. / Oh, okay. Hi, new Dad.
jokes.setup: Monica announces the last-minute lineup changes — Joey is officiating, Chandler is giving Phoebe away
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately calls Chandler 'new Dad' — a callback to Joey having been 'Dad' all episode, now casually transferred to Chandler
jokes.explanation: A quick, warm callback to the Joey-as-dad running gag. 'Hi, new Dad' works because it's breezy — Phoebe doesn't attach much significance to the swap, which is itself funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: Is it okay I want you to wear that headset in bed? / I have you scheduled for nudity at 2300 hours. / Oh, yeah.
jokes.setup: Monica is back in full wedding-commander mode with her headset, barking orders; Chandler finds this attractive
jokes.punchline: Monica schedules their sexual encounter in military time — '2300 hours' — maintaining the military-planner persona even when planning sex
jokes.explanation: A perfect capper on the Monica military-time running gag — she extends it into their sex life with 'I have you scheduled for nudity at 2300 hours.' The joke works because it's consistent with Monica's character (even intimacy gets time-blocked), it's a callback to the running gag, and 'nudity at 2300 hours' has a great rhythm. Chandler's 'Oh, yeah' approval is the right button.

jokes.text: Jeez, Ross. You could've showered. / It's the dog.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are walking in the wedding procession; apparently there's a bad smell
jokes.punchline: Chandler accuses Ross of not showering; Ross clarifies it's Chappy the dog — a quick, good visual/smell comedy beat
jokes.explanation: A quick bit with good economy (four words total). The structure is clean — accusation, correction. It's a simple but effective moment during what would otherwise be a straight scene. The humor is in Chandler's confidence in blaming Ross and Ross's matter-of-fact correction.

jokes.text: Groomsman? Why are you standing there? Where's your bridesmaid? / We've got a broken arrow! Bridesmaid down! / Oh, that's me.
jokes.setup: During the ceremony procession, there's a gap — a groomsman without his bridesmaid counterpart
jokes.punchline: Monica calls it a 'broken arrow! Bridesmaid down!' in full military crisis mode; Rachel belatedly realizes 'Oh, that's me' — she's the bridesmaid who fell down or is out of position
jokes.explanation: 'Broken arrow! Bridesmaid down!' is Monica at peak military-operations mode. The fact that it's describing a bridesmaid being late/fallen rather than a combat casualty is a great tonal collision. Rachel's 'Oh, that's me' is the perfect oblivious button.

jokes.text: Wow. Aren't you gonna be cold? / I don't care. / I'll be my 'something blue.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe appears at the top of the stairs, apparently in a dress that exposes her significantly to the cold winter air
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'I'll be my something blue' — she'll turn blue from cold, fulfilling the 'something blue' wedding tradition
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most elegant jokes. The 'something blue' wedding tradition pun works on two levels — Phoebe will literally be blue from hypothermia, fulfilling the tradition — and it's delivered with Phoebe's characteristically eccentric and breezy commitment. The joke is clever, character-specific (only Phoebe would think of this), and has great economy. High quotability. Earns close to 8.

jokes.text: Friends. Family. Dog. Thank you all for being here to witness this blessed event.
jokes.setup: Joey begins the wedding ceremony with the traditional opening words
jokes.punchline: He adds 'Dog' to 'Friends. Family.' — acknowledging Chappy as a third category of attendee, delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: 'Friends. Family. Dog.' is a beautiful comedic construction — the third item in the series breaks the rhythm and category in the perfect way. Joey's solemnity makes it funnier; he's not making a joke, he's sincerely including Chappy. Very economical. The callback to Chappy as a wedding participant pays off nicely here.

jokes.text: The cold has now spread to my special place, so I'm gonna do the short version of this.
jokes.setup: Joey is officiating the outdoor winter wedding; he's freezing
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals that the cold has reached his genitals ('my special place') and uses this as justification for skipping parts of the ceremony
jokes.explanation: 'My special place' is a great euphemism — childlike language in an adult context, delivered by Joey with his characteristic mixture of TMI and innocence. Using genital cold as an official reason to shorten a wedding ceremony is absurdist but grounded in physical reality. Good Joey voice.

jokes.text: And may they have many children who will one day avenge their family's honor. / How could I not get that part? Stupid Ralph Macchio.
jokes.setup: Joey is delivering the wedding blessing; he inserts a line about children avenging the family's honor — clearly from his failed Mafia movie audition
jokes.punchline: 'How could I not get that part? Stupid Ralph Macchio' — Joey reveals the competing actor and can't help voicing his competitive grievance mid-ceremony
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments and a perfect callback payoff. The escalation: Joey used audition lines on Mike (earlier), then in the ceremony blessing ('avenge their family's honor'), then breaks the fourth wall of the ceremony to complain about Ralph Macchio getting the part. 'Stupid Ralph Macchio' as a mid-wedding grievance is completely unexpected and very specific — Ralph Macchio as the Karate Kid is a beloved figure, making Joey's professional jealousy of him darkly funny. High quotability, great character integration, and the callback structure is excellent. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Oh, wait! Oh, I forgot. And... I love you. And you have nice eyes.
jokes.setup: Mike has just delivered a genuinely moving, romantic wedding speech; there's a sweet pause
jokes.punchline: Mike suddenly remembers he forgot something — 'I love you' (the most important thing) — delivered as an afterthought, then 'and you have nice eyes' as a kicker that deflates the grandeur
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant romantic-comedy joke. Mike's vows build to a beautiful moment, then he reveals the most fundamental declaration ('I love you') as a forgotten footnote, and closes with the banal but sweet 'you have nice eyes.' The joke works emotionally too — it's sweet AND funny, which is the right register for a wedding episode climax.

jokes.text: Joey? / Yeah? / Chappy's heart rate has slowed way down.
jokes.setup: During the wedding vows, apparently Chappy the elderly dog is in distress from the cold
jokes.punchline: 'Chappy's heart rate has slowed way down' — an extremely dark joke about the dog potentially dying during the wedding ceremony
jokes.explanation: A dark beat that works because Phoebe delivers it calmly mid-vows — a dog may be dying at her wedding and she pauses the ceremony to report it to the officiant. The clinical 'heart rate has slowed way down' is funny in its medical precision. Darkly comic and character-specific (Phoebe is simultaneously caring enough to notice and pragmatic enough to flag it without panicking).

jokes.text: I got married!
jokes.setup: Joey pronounces Phoebe and Mike husband and wife; they kiss
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's immediate exclamation 'I got married!' — the joy is undeniable but the phrasing sounds like someone who just won a game show
jokes.explanation: 'I got married!' is a great Phoebe exclamation — the past tense ('got' rather than 'am') and the excited disbelief make it funny and sweet simultaneously. It sounds like she's surprised it worked. Very Phoebe, great economy (three words), and in the moment it would get a big warm reaction from the audience.

jokes.text: Could someone get me a coat? I'm frigging freezing.
jokes.setup: Phoebe just had her romantic outdoor winter wedding in a bare-shouldered gown
jokes.punchline: The 'something blue' joke from earlier pays off — she's cold — delivered with Phoebe's characteristic anticlimax
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the 'something blue' joke. Phoebe's immediate pivot from romantic moment ('I got married!') to practical complaint ('I'm frigging freezing') is funny in its speed. 'Frigging' is a good Phoebe-ism. The scene structure — romantic peak immediately followed by physical discomfort — is classic sitcom.

jokes.text: It's 2300 hours and I'm about to have the most organized sex anyone's ever had.
jokes.setup: Joey invites people in for a drink; Monica declines and explains she has plans
jokes.punchline: 'I'm about to have the most organized sex anyone's ever had' — the callback to 'nudity at 2300 hours' and the culmination of Monica's entire military-planner arc
jokes.explanation: A great closing joke. 'The most organized sex anyone's ever had' is Monica-perfect — it's funny, specific, true to her character, and closes both the military-planner arc and the Chandler/Monica subplot of the episode. The phrasing 'most organized sex' is unusual enough to be very quotable. Strong callback, high character integration, leaves the audience on a laugh.

jokes.text: It's 2300 hours and I'm about to have the most organized sex anyone's ever had.
jokes.setup: Joey invites Monica and Chandler in for a drink after the wedding. Monica demurs.
jokes.punchline: Monica references 'nudity at 2300 hours' from earlier in the episode — revealing that she has actually scheduled sex on her wedding planning timeline.
jokes.explanation: 'The most organized sex anyone's ever had' is a great line — it's the logical conclusion of Monica's military planner persona and a satisfying callback. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Whatever happened to Ross? / I don't know. Maybe he hooked up with that hot girl he talked to. / Come on, Chappy! Do your business! / Make! / I did not sign on for this.
jokes.setup: The episode's final beat: Ross is left holding Chappy on a cold New York street
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'I did not sign on for this' — having gone from wanting to be a groomsman to being a dog-walker/scooper at midnight in a blizzard
jokes.explanation: A satisfying final button on Ross's episode arc. His entire story was about desperately wanting to be part of the wedding — and he ends up alone with the dog in a snowstorm. 'I did not sign on for this' is a great closing line — it's both a character-specific complaint and a broader commentary on how the episode went for him. The misdirection of possibly 'hooking up with a hot girl' vs. the reality of dog-walking is a good structural inversion.

tmdb_overview: As the big day approaches, Phoebe's wedding planner, Monica, makes everyone around her crazy because according to her - every little thing needs to happen around schedule. This doesn't sit well with Phoebe and she fires her. Unfortunately, on the wedding day New York is hit with the worst snowstorm its seen in 20 years, forcing plans to change. As a substitute for Phoebe's incarcerated father, Joey takes his role much too seriously. Meanwhile, Chandler and Ross discover that neither of them has a part in the wedding; however, after one of Mike's groomsmen is unable to attend, they compete for the open position by any means necessary.
insight: Phoebe's wedding softens the series—cringe drops, character beats rise to 77.
